drills.q: You assign obj.__add__ = my_func on an instance, expecting `obj + other` to use it. It doesn't. Why?
drills.a: Operators dispatch through type(obj).__add__, never through the instance's __dict__. Only ordinary explicit method calls (obj.method()) check the instance dict first; implicitly-invoked dunder/protocol methods always go through the type.

drills.q: A property with no setter raises AttributeError on obj.name = 'x' instead of quietly creating an instance attribute. Explain the mechanism.
drills.a: property is a data descriptor -- it implements __set__ even without an explicit setter (the default raises AttributeError). Data descriptors always outrank instance __dict__ during assignment, so the write is intercepted rather than falling through to obj.__dict__.

drills.q: A class combines two library base classes and Python raises 'TypeError: metaclass conflict.' What's happening and what are your options?
drills.a: The two base classes have unrelated metaclasses, and neither is a subclass of the other, so Python can't auto-resolve a single consistent metaclass. Fix: define your own metaclass inheriting from both conflicting metaclasses and pass it explicitly -- but only safe if the two metaclasses' behaviors are actually compatible, not just compatible in type hierarchy.

drills.q: Derive the MRO for D(B, C) where B(A) and C(A), and explain why naive depth-first search gets it wrong.
drills.a: C3 linearization gives [D, B, C, A, object]. Naive DFS gives [D, B, A, C, A, object], letting A resolve before C is even consulted -- violating local precedence order, since D explicitly listed B before C, implying C (and only unshadowed parts of A) should resolve before A itself is reached.

drills.q: functools.cached_property stops caching (recomputes every access) once a class adopts __slots__. Why?
drills.a: cached_property is a non-data descriptor that caches its computed value directly into instance.__dict__ on first access, relying on the precedence rule (instance __dict__ beats non-data descriptors) for later accesses to skip __get__. A class using __slots__ has no instance __dict__ to write into unless a matching slot is explicitly added.

drills.q: You're designing a plugin system where every Plugin subclass should auto-register itself. Would you use __init_subclass__ or a metaclass, and when would that choice flip?
drills.a: __init_subclass__ by default -- it handles 'run logic when a subclass is defined' without metaclass-conflict risk for downstream consumers combining Plugin with other base classes. Flip to a metaclass only if you need to modify the class's namespace/attributes BEFORE the class object is constructed (e.g., injecting a method the class body itself references), which __init_subclass__ runs too late to do.

drills.q: A class overrides __eq__ but not __hash__ and becomes unhashable. Explain why Python does this defensively, and whether a constant-value __hash__ is a valid fix.
drills.a: Python requires equal objects to hash equal for dict/set correctness; the inherited identity-based __hash__ would likely violate this once __eq__ changes semantics, so Python sets __hash__=None automatically. A constant __hash__ is technically valid (never violates the invariant) but destroys hash table performance -- every instance collides into the same bucket, degrading dict/set ops to O(n).

drills.q: Does CPython 3.11+'s specializing adaptive interpreter change any observable behavior of dunder dispatch or descriptor precedence?
drills.a: No -- it's a pure internal execution optimization that caches/specializes bytecode for observed types at a call site, transparently falling back to general dispatch if a different type appears. The data model's semantics (what value operations produce, which method resolves) are unchanged; only speed differs.
